extracted.intended_audience: Reuters journalists, correspondents and sub-editors (including sports reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: A Reuters stylebook covering general news-writing rules (usage, spelling, punctuation, bias avoidance, datelines, proper names) and a sports-specific style guide giving conventions for speed, tone, statistics, measurements and sport-specific terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand juries: function and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Their prime function is to review evidence presented by a prosecutor and determine whether there is probable cause to return an indictment. Under the constitution, a grand jury indictment is required for federal criminal charges. Only about half of the states' judicial systems use grand juries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as background when relevant; do not assume every state uses grand juries.

rubrics_metrics.name: New York Supreme Court: clarify court level
rubrics_metrics.description: Note: the New York Supreme Court is a trial court, not the highest court in the state (the Court of Appeals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make this clear in copy; equate it roughly to district/superior/circuit courts elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. datelines that stand alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The following U.S. cities stand alone in a dateline without the need to mention their state: Atlanta, Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Dallas, Denver, Detroit, Honolulu, Houston, Indianapolis, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, Milwauke, Minneapolis, New Orleans, New York, Oklahoma City, Philadelphia, Phoenix, Pittsburg, St Louis, Salt Lake City, San Antonio, San Diego, San Francisco, Seattle, Washington.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these city names alone in datelines; for other cities include state.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Marshals Service punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: No apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write U.S. Marshals Service (not Marshal's or Marshals').

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. legislative titles: first and subsequent references
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not abbreviate legislative titles in the United States. Use Governor, Senator, Representative at first mention and then refer to the politician by surname on subsequent reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include the district or state that the legislator represents unless context-essential. Refrain from calling senators 'senior' or 'junior'; political leaning is more relevant than seniority.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. states / commonwealths reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Strictly speaking, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Virginia are commonwealths, but we should refer to them as states. Their constitutional status is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as states in copy; note Louisiana uses parishes rather than counties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain phrasing: 'user friendly'
rubrics_metrics.description: Jargon. Prefer easy to use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace 'user friendly' with 'easy to use' and similar plain-language choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simpler spelling: 'utilise'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change 'utilise' to 'use' unless there is a compelling reason not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versus usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell it out in full in text. It can be abbreviated to vs in tables, but American style is to use v. in court cases, e.g. Roe v. Wade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'versus' in prose; 'vs' in tables; 'v.' for U.S. court cases per American style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing 'veteran' in sports/general news
rubrics_metrics.description: Overused in sports and general news stories and best avoided. Be more precise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the person’s age and the details that show why the person is a veteran instead of relying on the label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vietnamese names: second-reference rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the last name alone at second reference, e.g. Nguyen Co Thach is Thach and Bui Tin is Tin. The only exception is Ho Chi Minh (nom de guerre) who is Ho at second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this pattern to avoid confusion; exceptions noted explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: vice- hyphenation and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate titles such as vice-president, vice-admiral, vice-chairman etc, apart from U.S. titles. In American style, use two words for titles such as vice admiral, vice chairman, vice secretary. Hyphenate vice-president unless U.S. usage, e.g. vice president of the United States or of an American company. Capitalise when immediately preceding the name of a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust hyphenation and capitalization based on U.S. vs other usage and position in sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Videogame spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: One word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'videogame' (one word).

rubrics_metrics.name: VAT definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Value added tax, a system of taxing products on the value added at each stage of production and exchange, effectively a consumption tax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out on first reference as necessary; use 'VAT' subsequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virgin Mary phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use this title or the Madonna, not Our Lady except in titles such as Our Lady of Czestochowa or in the names of churches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Virgin Mary' or 'the Madonna' in prose; 'Our Lady' only in proper names/titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocal cords spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Not chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'vocal cords' when referring to the anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice mails spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'voice mails' (two words).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcano plural
rubrics_metrics.description: volcano, volcanoes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard plural 'volcanoes'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of wrack vs rack
rubrics_metrics.description: Use wrack only for seaweed and 'wrack and ruin'. Otherwise use rack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply correct word choice based on meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing: prefer simpler, concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the familiar word to the far-fetched. Prefer the short word to the long and the single word to the circumlocution. Prefer the concrete word to the abstract. Prefer the Saxon word to the Romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid pompous words (ongoing, escalating, prestigious, meaningful, facility) and other overwrought language; choose clarity and brevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories relying heavily on phrases that have become stale through over use are like paintings done by number. They convey information but lack life or freshness. Avoid clichés that exaggerate or over-simplify e.g. the postage-stamp country, the oil-rich sheikhdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long list of common clichés (diplomacy, disasters, violence, industrial trouble) should be avoided; prefer specific concrete description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid euphemism
rubrics_metrics.description: Euphemism seeks to cloak reality. Shun it. Except in quotation, write elderly people not senior citizens; kill not terminate with extreme prejudice; poor not disadvantaged, died of cancer not passed away after a fight with cancer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct, plain language rather than euphemism except in quotes or when necessary for sensitivity with sourcing/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jargon or explain it
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical and professional jargon has no place on the Reuters file unless you are writing for a narrow, specialist audience and are certain the story is not likely to interest a broader readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either avoid jargon or explain it in simple terms; paraphrase jargon-laced quotes; don't use newsroom jargon like 'stringer' — use 'freelance journalist'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid long words and clumsy titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unnecessarily long words and clumsy strings of names and titles. Split up long names and titles for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break up long sequences (e.g., 'Under-Secretary for Military Procurement, Major-General Abdul Karim al-Razzak' or similar constructions). Prefer shorter synonyms listed in the guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simpler synonyms where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide simpler alternatives (e.g., additional -> more; approximately -> about; demonstrate -> show; establish -> set up; numerous -> many).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace listed formal words with their simpler synonyms unless precision requires otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphors: use fresh, avoid mixed or absurd metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A fresh and vivid metaphor can add much to a story. But avoid mixed metaphors and metaphors whose literal sense is absurd (e.g., 'a growing bottleneck').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors sparingly and ensure they are coherent and literal sense is sensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive repetition of words and stereotyped descriptions, but do not overdo variation to the point of awkwardness. Repeating organisational names can be better than awkward substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance avoidance of repetition with clarity (e.g., better to repeat 'United Nations' than use an obscure substitute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reported speech tense rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not retain the present indicative in reported speech. Change is to was; are to were; will/shall to would; has/have to had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: In news agency style, lead paragraphs with the source at the end may keep present tense for clarity (example provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spin and loaded names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin can be insidious and subliminal, conveyed in words and phrases that disguise an agenda. Example: 'Operation Iraqi Freedom' named by the U.S. should be reported as 'the United States invaded Iraq to overthrow Saddam Hussein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer neutral, descriptive language; avoid adopting promotional or partisan labels without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb selection and neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbs bring action and life but the wrong verb can indicate bias. The verb 'to say' is usually the best neutral choice. Some verbs (alleged, claimed, maintained, noted, pointed out, emphasised) carry implication; use announced with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid verbs that imply disbelief or attribution unless supported; avoid 'concede' (implies admission), 'refute' (means disprove) when you mean 'deny'. Don't use limp constructions like 'the fire left six people dead' — use active clear verbs (fires killed six people). Avoid 'continued/ongoing' in lead paragraphs; avoid 'to get'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writeoff noun/verb form
rubrics_metrics.description: One word as a noun, two words as a verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'writeoff' as noun, 'write off' as verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: World Wide Web / Web capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Shorten to Web, but website, webcast, webmaster are lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize 'Web' when used as shorthand for World Wide Web; keep 'website' lowercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports style overarching aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters sports service needs to be fast, informative, reliable, accurate and entertaining. Sport moves markets and is entertainment; coverage should reflect speed, breadth, personalities and statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely stories including run-up and aftermath, profiles of personalities, and reliable statistics/historical data delivered clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports style: consistency and clarity in stats and terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: For Reuters to keep its reputation for accuracy, correspondents and sub-editors need to be consistent and clear in the way they report and handle news and statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sports guide alongside the general style guide; be consistent across copy, especially for frequently used sports items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: measurement and conversion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Sport uses only metric measurements except for American sport and golf where yards and feet are used and sailing where nautical miles are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In boxing with U.S. fighters aimed at a U.S. market, imperial conversions for height/weight may be added; otherwise use metric. All currencies must show a conversion into dollars at first reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: avoid clichés and tired hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports reporting is vulnerable to cliché; many overused phrases should be avoided (e.g., 'crash out', 'crucial', 'hard fought', 'icon', 'legend', 'major', 'star', 'veteran', etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific description rather than stock phrases; a list of common clichés is provided to avoid repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: contractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid contractions such as couldn't, didn't, wasn't, can't in copy except in direct speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write out full forms (could not, did not) unless quoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: head/term capitalization and titling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitals are used where the title is attributed directly to a named individual (e.g., 'FIFA President Sepp Blatter said...') but not when the title alone is used ('The president said...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply capitalization depending on attribution and usage in the sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: team/verb agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teams take a singular verb (e.g. New York is playing San Francisco, the team is on the road) except teams with plural names take plural verbs (e.g. The Chicago Bears are in town).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose verb number based on whether the team name is singular collective or explicitly plural in form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: game vs match / field vs pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use 'match' for American sports — use 'game'. Baseball and American football are played on fields not pitches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sport-appropriate terminology (game/field for U.S. sports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: MVP abbreviation and first reference
rubrics_metrics.description: MVP — Most valuable player — spelt out at first reference, then abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At first mention write out 'most valuable player' then use 'MVP' subsequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: inning/innings usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Inning singular, innings plural (unlike cricket where both singular and plural are 'innings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct singular/plural forms depending on sport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: use of 'as' conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As' is overused and can link loosely connected developments; it often leads to clumsy or misleading sentences and implies continuing action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer splitting sentences or using 'and' instead; don't use 'as' to describe sudden events — use clearer constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: conversions for distances and currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use metric measurements generally; in boxing involving U.S. fighters aimed at a U.S. market imperial conversions may be added. All currencies must show a conversion into dollars at first reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide conversions only where audience expectations dictate; always include dollar conversions first time a currency is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: use of 'crowd' grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: crowd - Takes a singular verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use singular verb agreement with 'crowd' (e.g., The crowd was... ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: 'disaster' and 'tragedy' avoid in sporting contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'disaster' or 'tragedy' for sporting contests because this devalues the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve such words for genuinely catastrophic events (e.g., stadium collapses), not for losing a match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: 'hat-trick' and hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: hat-trick - Hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyphenated 'hat-trick' in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: honorifics and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use titles in sports stories. Don Bradman and Alex Ferguson, not Sir Don and Sir Alex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid honorifics and knighthoods in sports copy to keep tone plain and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports: 'icon' banned on sports file
rubrics_metrics.description: Icon - Banned on the sports file for describing sporting figures. Use only in religious contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hyperbolic labels like 'icon' when describing athletes; prefer factual descriptors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling and small word usage: specific entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Various single-word style prescriptions (e.g., 'wagon' not 'waggon'; 'walkie-talkie' hyphen; 'weekend' not 'week-end'; 'weather forecaster' not 'weatherman'; 'wind farm' two words; 'workforce' one word; 'word processor' no hyphen; 'worldwide' no hyphen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed spellings and hyphenation choices consistently in copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather terms: defined usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide clear definitions and uses for common weather terms (e.g., anticyclone, blizzard, Beaufort Scale, cyclone, depression, El Niño/La Niña, Fahrenheit/Celsius usage, hurricane/typhoon/cyclone naming conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate meteorological definitions and correct regional naming conventions; convert temps appropriately and explain phenomena when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and church references (Western Wall, Our Lady, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Western Wall' not 'Wailing Wall'. Use 'Our Lady' only in proper names; 'Virgin Mary' or 'the Madonna' otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer established/recommended titles and avoid colloquial or potentially offensive alternatives.
